description: NGC 1761 is an open cluster located in the constellation Dorado, a small and fainted constellation whose stars do not exceed magnitude 3. Cluster NGC 1761 has an apparent magnitude between 9 and 10. The cluster is located in the Large Cloud of Magellan, in the N11 region, home to several nebulae and open star clusters.
name: NGC 1761

description:
"Tucked away in a dark region of the famed Orion, the hunter Constellation is the delicate cosmic cloud called NGC 1788.
Found not too far beyond the bright star Rigel, this isolated dusty cocoon is known as a reflection nebula - a type of cloud of gas and dust that appears to shine thanks to scattering light radiating out from a nearby cluster of stars. While the nebulosity overall appearance is compact and elongated it is contained within a keystone configuration of four stars, the brightest of which is only 10th magnitude.
Look for an almost round, central bright core that is wrapped in wispy filaments stretching out into surrounding dark expanse of interstellar space."
name: NGC 1788

description: NGC 185, also known as Caldwell 18, is a dwarf galaxy in the Cassiopeia constellation. Looking like a flattened balloon, it measures between 10,000 and 12,000 light-years in diameter for a weight of 660 million Suns. The galaxy is in fact a satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy M31. The stars in the outer reaches of the galaxy formed more than a billion years ago. In the central regions, however, the galaxy still seems to be forming new stars as demonstrated by the presence of young star clusters.
name: NGC 185

description: NGC 1851, also known as Caldwell 73, is a globular cluster in the constellation Columba. The mass of the cluster is estimated to be 550,000 times the mass of the Sun, spread over an estimated 200,000 stars. This number of stars is equivalent to the brown bear population in the world. The stars in the cluster are about 10 billion years old and did not all form at the same time. Two different populations were identified with very old, red stars and younger, more massive, hotter, blue stars. Researchers are trying to understand how these two populations came to be.
name: NGC 1851

description: NGC 188 is located in the constellation Cepheus and is circumpolar, meaning it is so close to the North Celestial Pole that it is above the horizon at all times from anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. It is estimated to be over 4 billion years old, making it one of the oldest open clusters known in the Milky Way.
name: NGC 188

description: IC 2118 is a reflection nebula in Eridan, illuminated by the bright star Rigel. This nebula is pretty faint but also very large. It got its nickname of Witch Head Nebula as in photographs, the nebula looks like the profile of a witch. IC 2118 was discovered by William Herschel in 1786.
name: Witch Head Nebula

description: The Fly Nebula, also known as NGC 1931, is an open cluster embedded in an emission and reflection nebula in the Auriga constellation. A massive star of about 8 solar masses formed in the region 25 million years ago. Its intense radiation causes the surrounding nebulae to glow either blue when the light is simply reflected or red if it is absorbed and re-emitted by the gas. The gas and dust region was disrupted and new young stars less than 2 million years old are forming.
name: Fly Nebula

description: "NGC 1955 is a star cluster associated with an emission nebula found in the Dorado constellation, more precisely, near the Large Magellanic Cloud, and only visible from the Southern Hemisphere. This is a region called H II (read H 2, characterized by very extensive, hydrogen charged clouds; most of its atoms are ionized (modified atomic structure) when they come into contact with the clusters' stars."
name: NGC 1955

description: "The Running Man Nebula is a cloud of interstellar gas and dust located in the constellation Orion, in the Hunter's Sword area. Unlike its neighbor the Orion M42 nebula, this object is dominated by blue colors coming from interstellar dust reflecting the light emitted by hot young stars from this region."
name: Running Man Nebula

description: NGC 2014 is an emission nebula associated with a star cluster found in the constellation Dorado and more precisely, in the region of the Large Magellanic Cloud, visible only from the Southern Hemisphere. Called stellar nurseries, emission nebulae are home to stars so massive and energetic that they sculpt the envelope of gas and dust that surrounds them.
name: NGC 2014

description: Detected in photographs in 1888, along with the Horsehead nebula and NGC 2023, the Flame nebula is an emission nebula that is part of the Orion Molecular Cloud Complex. A cluster of young, still forming stars is present in the center of the Flame, but is not actually visible to amateur observers.
name: Flame Nebula

description: The Tarantula nebula is a huge, bright object located in the Large Magellanic Cloud, outside of the Milky Way galaxy. The nebula is so huge and bright that if it were as close to us as the famous Orion nebula, you would be able to see your shadows when it rises in the sky. The nebula was discovered by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille while he was traveling to the Cape of Good Hope.
name: Tarantula Nebula

description:
"NGC 2141 is a rich open cluster hiding out in the constellation Orion’s raised club. Discovered by American astronomer Edward Barnard in 1883, it resides at a distance of approximately 13,200 light years from our Solar System.
Its age, estimated at 1.7 billion years, is complemented by an apparent size in the sky equivalent to one-third of the moon's disk, while its actual size in space spans about 38.3 light years. Unlike many young star clusters throughout the Milky Way, NGC 2141 mysteriously lacks an abundance of youthful blue stars, and instead showcases a nearly equal blend with red stars, which may indicate the cluster gravitationally may have captured, foreign stars and incorporated them into the cluster.
This celestial gathering is not only a captivating sight but also strategically positioned near the celestial equator. As a result, observers from both Northern and Southern hemispheres can enjoy glimpses of its stellar splendours."
name: NGC 2141

description:
"The Little Pleiades, also known as NGC 2169, is an open cluster in the Orion constellation. The cluster is sometimes called the 37 Cluster because the stars appear to form that number in the sky.

According to the most recent data from the Gaia Mission, the cluster consists of at least 65 stars. The stars are estimated to be 9 million years old. They are moving away from us at a speed of 100,000 km/h, that is, 3.5 times faster than the ISS."
name: Little Pleiades

description: NGC 2174 is an emission nebula associated with a star cluster that can be found in the Orion constellation, above the red supergiant star Betelgeuse. Located about 6400 light-years from Earth, it is 4 times farther away than its neighbor the Orion Nebula. We can also see, in front of the gas cloud of the nebula, the young star cluster NGC 2175 whose age is estimated at 9 million years.
name: Monkey Head Nebula

description: The Rosette nebula is a beautiful object in Monoceros that is very difficult to see visually. It is home to a young cluster of stars, NGC 2244, that formed within the gases a million years ago. This cluster is, unlike the nebula itself, very easy to spot in the night sky and you may even be able to see it without any instrument. The Rosette nebula is massive, colorful, and full of details, which makes it a fantastic target to photograph.
name: Rosette Nebula

description: "NGC 2261 was the targeted object for the Hale telescope's first light at Mount Palomar observatory on January 26, 1949, 20 years after it began construction in 1928. It was Edwin Hubble who manipulated the telescope. He had previously studied the nebula at Yerkes Observatory and Mount Wilson Observatory."
name: "Hubble's Variable Nebula"

description: "Located in the constellation Monoceros (the Unicorn), NGC2264 actually designates two astronomical objects: the Cone, a diffuse nebula located in the south, and the Christmas Tree, a young star cluster located in the north. NGC2264's brightest star is S Monocerotis."
name: Cone nebula / Christmas Tree cluster

description: NGC 2281 is an open cluster in the Auriga constellation. The latest studies based on data from the Gaia mission have confirmed that at least 400 stars belong to the cluster. Unlike many open clusters, there does not appear to be a concentration of stars in the center of the cluster. This one is 650 million years old. Consequently, stars three times more massive than the Sun are already dead.
name: NGC 2281

description:
"NGC 2298 is a globular cluster in the Puppis constellation. The first stars in this cluster formed 12.7 billion years ago. Currently, the mass of this cluster is estimated to be 50,000 times that of the Sun. It decreases regularly because the cluster is breaking apart and losing stars. It has already lost 85% of its original mass, and the ejected stars form what is called a tidal tail; a kind of filament attached to the cluster. This structure is not visible on the image. 
The stars in the cluster are moving away from us at a speed of 147 km/s or 529,200 km/h. In other words, the stars are moving 500 times faster than an airliner."
name: NGC 2298

description: Thor’s Helmet is a cloud of interstellar gas that has the shape of Thor’s Helmet. Although it is a faint target and is not really impressive when observing, the colors in the gases really pop when taking long exposure shots with a camera. This beautiful deep-sky object gets its glow from WR7, a massive Wolf-Rayet star that will soon turn into a supernova.
name: "Thor's Helmet"

description:
"NGC 2360, also known as Caroline's Cluster, is an open star cluster located in the constellation Canis Major, approximately 3,700 light-years away from Earth.

This cluster contains approximately 60 relatively young stars, with an estimated age of around 60 million years."
name: "Caroline's Cluster"

description: Also listed as Caldwell 64, this young cluster located in the constellation Canis Major contains several hundred stars. The brightest star is Tau Canis Majoris, a supergiant 50 times more massive than our Sun.
name: Tau Canis Majoris Cluster

description: Also called the Peanut Nebula, NGC 2371 is a planetary nebula with 3 main structural features: two diametrically opposite lobes and a central peanut-like enveloppe. The dying star responsible for this chaotic event has now reached the extremely hot surface temperature of approximately 100,000 degrees. This high temperature produces a highly energetic UV radiation that heats up the neighboring gas and causes it to glow in the visible light domain. In NGC 2371’s case, the emitted blue light indicates a rich concentration of oxygen.
name: Gemini Nebula

description: The Eskimo Nebula is a bipolar planetary nebula with a double shell. It is located in the constellation Gemini.
name: Eskimo Nebula

description: NGC 2403 is a spiral galaxy located 11 million light-years away from the Milky Way, in the constellation Camelopardalis, the Giraffe. The northern spiral arm is home to a giant star-forming region, NGC 2404, an open star cluster associated with an emission nebula. Bright stars, part of our own Milky Way, are visible in the foreground.
name: NGC 2403

description:
"Located in the Lynx constellation, the star cluster NGC 2419 is estimated to be 10 million years old. It is one of the most distant globular clusters of the Milky Way in our solar system, which explains a lower luminosity than other better-known clusters such as Omega Centauri, located at 160,000 A.L.

The position of the 3 stars HD 60771, double star HD 60694 and TYC 2958-870-1, near the globular cluster, reminds the shape of the Big Dipper's handle."
name: Intergalactic Wanderer

description: NGC 246, also known as Caldwell 56 or the Skull Nebula, is a planetary nebula in the Cetus Constellation. It formed 6,600 years ago when the outer layers of a star, with an initial mass of 4.3 solar masses, were ejected. The nebula grows at a speed of about 35km/s, although its rate of expansion slows as it comes into contact with the interstellar medium. This shell of oxygen and hydrogen-rich material has already reached 2.1 light-years in size.
name: Skull Nebula

description: NGC 2467 is an emission nebula associated with a star cluster, or rather a superposition of several groups of stars located on the same line of sight, at different distances. We observe in this stellar nursery young stars at different stages of formation, young stars whose birth nebula has already dispersed, stars detaching from their cocoon of birth gas or stars that have just been formed.
name: Skull and Crossbones Nebula

description: NCC 247, or Caldwell 62, is an intermediate spiral galaxy in the Cetus Constellation. It is 70,000 light-years across and has a mass equivalent to 75 billion Suns. It belongs to the Sculptor group of galaxies, dominated by the larger NGC 253 and NGC 300 galaxies. Caldwell 62 has a gap in one of its arms and a recent study revealed that no stars have formed in this region over the last billion years, in contrast to those outside the hole. The gas in this region may have been removed by a gravitational interaction with another galaxy, preventing the birth of new stars.
name: NGC 247

description:
"The Electric Guitar Cluster, also known as the Termite Hole Cluster, Caldwell 71, or NGC 2477, is an open cluster in the Puppis constellation. At one billion years old, the cluster still contains 2,699 members according to the latest Gaia satellite data. It is therefore one of the most star-rich open clusters in the southern sky. In the sky, the cluster will appear slightly smaller in size than the full moon.
The cluster is moving away from us at 7.3 km/s, in other words, at over 26,000 km/h or the equivalent of a round trip from New York to Cape Town in one hour."
name: Electric Guitar Cluster

description: NGC 2506, also known as Caldwell 54, is an open cluster in the Monoceros constellation. Based on data from the Gaia mission, 1487 stars belong to this cluster. The stars are estimated to be 1.6 billion years old. In the cluster, an estimated 40% of the stars are not alone but in fact, belong to a binary system. The stars live in pairs. As in the case of many clusters, we find stars called blue stragglers. In the case of NGC 2506, there are 14 stars hotter and more massive than the rest of its members. They appear blue compared to the other stars.
name: NGC 2506

description: NGC 2516, also known as the Caldwell 96 or the Sprinter Cluster, is an open star cluster in the Carina Constellation. According to research, this cluster contains at least 800 stars that are roughly 175 million years old. The stars present have masses reaching double that of the Sun and surface temperatures rising to 10,000°C. Some of them also have a luminosity of up to twenty times that of the Sun. The cluster looks like the Pleiades, with a comparable number of stars of similar age. That said, it is more distant and less easy to observe.
name: Sprinter Cluster

description: NGC 253 is a starburst galaxy, experiencing extreme star formation, in the constellation of Sculptor. The Sculptor Galaxy is one of the brightest galaxies in the sky, and is easily observable with any kind of instrument.
name: Sculptor Galaxy

description: NGC 2683 is a spiral galaxy in the Lynx constellation. The galaxy is moving away from us at a speed of 410 km/s. The galaxy contains about 300 globular clusters, twice the known number found in the Milky Way. It is surrounded by at least 4 satellite galaxies, the largest of which is 12,000 light-years in diameter or ⅔ the size of the Small Magellanic Cloud. The near edge-on galaxy is considerably reddened by the dust and cold gas clouds it contains.
name: NGC 2683

description: The Pencil Nebula is a small part of the Vela Supernova Remnant, located near the Vela Pulsar in the constellation Vela. Its elongated appearance seemed made of braided filaments which are actually long ripples in a cosmic sheet of glowing gas seen almost edge-on. Its source supernova exploded approximately 12,000 years ago, creating a shock wave which now plows through space at over 500,000 kilometers per hour, which accounts for the unusual shape of the nebula.
name: Pencil Nebula

description: NGC 2775 is a spiral galaxy located in the constellation Cancer, approximately 67 million light-years away from Earth. It is also known as Caldwell 48. With a diameter of about 90,000 light-years, it is estimated to have a mass of around 100 billion times that of the Sun.
name: Caldwell 48

description: NGC 2808 is a globular cluster located in the constellation Carina. It is 12.5 billion years old and can be observed from the southern hemisphere. NGC 2808 is one of the most massive star clusters in the Milky Way, and contains more than a million stars.
name: NGC 2808

description:
"NGC 281 is an emission nebula located in the Milky Way’s Perseus spiral arm.
The Pacman nebula got its name because it looks like a famous video game character when seen in wide field. The nebula has a young star cluster, IC 1590, within its star-forming region, which lights up the gases around it."
name: Pacman Nebula

description: Located in the Southern constellation of Sculptor, NGC 288 is a low-concentration globular cluster found by astronomer Willian Herschel in 1785. With a pair of binoculars, it can be observed in the same field as the popular Sculptor galaxy (NGC 253). NGC 288 is estimated to be 10 billion years old and located about 30,000 light-years from Earth.
name: NGC 288

description: NGC 2903 is a barred spiral galaxy located about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Leo. It was discovered in 1784 by William Herschel.
name: NGC 2903

description: Easily visible to the naked eye, the Small Magellanic Cloud, also known as NGC 292, is a dwarf galaxy in the Tucana constellation. It is the 4th closest extragalactic object to us at only 200,000 light-years away from our galaxy. This proximity means that this satellite galaxy, which was probably once a spiral galaxy, was deformed by interactions with the Milky Way to become irregular. We currently estimate that the SMC contains a few hundred million stars and weighs 7 billion solar masses. There is also a bridge of gas that connects it to the Large Magellanic Cloud, which is evidence of interaction between the two galaxies as well. This is a star-forming region.
name: Small Magellanic Cloud

description: NGC 2997 is a spiral galaxy belonging to a little-known constellation of the Southern sky whose name is Antlia. We owe this constellation to French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille who named it in the 1750’s when he travelled to the Southern Hemisphere. 40 years later, the illustrious British astronomer William Herschel observed NGC 2997 galaxy for the first time using his 17” telescope. NGC 2997 is a superb galaxy with white and blue spiral arms. It is located at 12 Megaparsec and its mass is estimated to 210 billion solar masses, about two times less than the Andromeda galaxy.
name: NGC 2997

description: NGC 300, also known as Caldwell 70, is a spiral galaxy in the Sculptor constellation. It is also called the Southern Pinwheel Galaxy because it resembles M101. With a diameter of 40,000 light-years, it is smaller than our galaxy. In the sky, its size represents ⅔ of the full Moon. As for mass, it is estimated to be 30 billion times that of the Sun. This galaxy does not have a central bulge - the very bright area densely populated with stars that we find in our galaxy.
name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy

description:
"NGC 3109 is an irregular dwarf galaxy located in the Hydra constellation - the widest spread constellation of our sky. This low surface brightness and details-poor galaxy is the primary member of a larger association group of galaxies discovered in 2006 and whose members are: Antlia, Sextans A and Sextans B. One suggests this galactic group would orbit the Milky Way and would be part of the local group.
A special property of NGC 3109 is its relative motion to our galaxy: it is moving outwards at a speed of 403 km/s. In addition to be dizzying, this figure is 105 km/s higher than what astronomers’ computations suggest. Some theories assume this galaxy would have gained such excess of speed while approaching the center of the Milky Way. NGC 3109 is thus part of a broad category of galaxies called “backsplashers” which have already crossed or passed by the center of mass of a galactic cluster or a galaxy."
name: NGC 3109

description: NGC 3114 is an open cluster in the Carina constellation. The roughly 130-million-year-old stars in this cluster are 2,250 light-years away from the Earth. The study of this region to determine which stars are part of the cluster is complicated by the presence of many field stars. It is currently estimated that the cluster contains at least 1,000 stars. In this relatively young cluster, Sun-like stars are at the very beginning of their several billion years of life while stars with a mass of more than 20 times that of the Sun have already disappeared.
name: NGC 3114

description:
"The Spindle galaxy is a very particular galaxy in the Sextant constellation. Located 31 million light-years away, its physical properties situate it halfway between a spiral galaxy and an elliptical galaxy. Emitting a very diffuse and evenly distributed light, NGC 3115 presents very little detail. It remains nevertheless a fascinating object for astronomers as it contains: a central disc-shaped nucleus, a fine ring structure with aborted spiral arms as well as a large population of globular clusters. It is the closest galaxy to the solar system according to these particular criteria.
In 1992, two American astronomers discovered a supermassive black hole using NASA's Chandra X-ray telescope. Its mass is estimated at 2 billion times that of the Sun!"
name: Spindle Galaxy

description:
"Like the Ring nebula in the Northern Hemisphere, the Southern Ring Nebula is a marvelous planetary nebula dedicated to southern observers and situated in the Vela constellation. Its name reflects its specific ellipsoid structure.
The star responsible for this ejection of hot gas is not the one we can easily spot at the center of the nebula in pictures made with amateur telescopes. The genuine star, a white dwarf whose surface temperature is averaging 100,000 degrees, is exclusively visible with professional telescopes because of its low brightness and proximity to its neighbor. Moreover, both stars do not appear close due to a line-of-sight effect: they are really close to each other since they are making a binary star system."
name: Southern Ring Nebula

description: NGC 3190 is a spiral galaxy in the Leo constellation. It is surrounded by the NGC 3185, NGC 3187, and NGC 3193 galaxies. These four galaxies form the Leo Quartet, also known as Hickson 44. These galaxies are about 80 million light-years away from us. NGC 3190 hosts a supermassive black hole within its core that weighs 126 million solar masses, which is about 30 times more massive than the Milky Way. The near edge-on galaxy appears yellow because the blue light emitted by the young stars is absorbed by the dust.
name: Leo Quartet

description: Informally named the Banana Nebula, NGC 3199 is an emission nebula found in the southern constellation Carina. The object’s bright crescent feature is part of a much larger but fainter bubble of gas and dust.
name: Banana Nebula

description: NGC3201 is a globular cluster, which unlike other clusters, concentrates relatively fewer stars in its center. The cumulative mass of all the stars of which it is composed is estimated at 250,000 times that of the Sun. Its age is estimated to be more than 10 billion years.
name: NGC 3201

description: Also known as the Eye Nebula, the Ghost of Jupiter has a size and shape very similar to the planet Jupiter. NGC 3242 a planetary nebula, is located in the Hydra constellation.
name: Ghost of Jupiter

description:
"NGC 3247, also known as RCW 49, is an emission nebula in the constellation Carina. The red nebula is produced by the massive young star cluster Westerlund 2. The stars in the cluster formed 2 million years ago and partially tore the gas shell of their nursery. With surface temperatures as high as 40,000°C and a luminosity 1,000,000 times that of the Sun, the twenty or so massive stars heat the gas in the NGC 3247 cloud. 
The image also contains the IC 2581 star cluster with what appears to be its blue-white stars. The cluster contains about 400 stars that are ten or so million years old. The supergiant variable star V399 Carinae is also found in this region, but its membership in the cluster is uncertain.
The image also contains WR 20a, which may or may not belong to Westerlund 2. This massive star is actually a binary system consisting of two Wolf-Rayet-type stars that orbit each other in 3.6 days. These stars have burned almost all their hydrogen and will enter their final stages of life in a few million years. With 83 and 82 solar masses, the stars in this system are among the five most massive stars known."
name: RCW 49

description: NGC 3293 is a young open cluster found in the Carina constellation. Lying at a distance of about 8000 light-years, it has a particularly high abundance of hot blue stars. Their age is estimated to be about 6 million years old, whereas the cluster’s dimmer, redder stars appear to be about 20 million years old.
name: Little Jewel Box Cluster

description:
"The open cluster NGC 3324 and associated emission nebula IC 2599 are two objects in the Carina constellation. IC 2599 is also known as the Gabriela Mistral Nebula. This nickname comes from the nebula’s resemblance to the Chilean poetess in profile.
Located at the edge of the Carina Nebula, the cluster contains 5 massive stars, among others. The intense UV radiation from these stars blows the gas and dust surrounding them away. It ended up carving out a cavity 20 light-years in diameter. On the edges of this irregularly shaped bubble, the gas is compressed, revealing a white color contrast in the gas-free areas, and elsewhere gradations of red depending on the amount of gas and dust, but also on the temperature at which the whole is heated. Finally, in the regions dense in gas but cold, we observe dark areas.
The first stars in the cluster are 10 million years old and new stars should appear in the rest of the molecular cloud."
name: Gabriel Mistral Nebula

description: NGC 3344 is a barred spiral galaxy wandering 20 million light-years away in the middle of the Leo Minor constellation. Even though its angular size is 5 times smaller than the apparent diameter of the moon, both its suitable orientation and stunning spiral arms call to contemplate it through an amateur telescope. Sprinkled with rich ionized hydrogen patches, NGC 3344 is also the home of supernovae remnants. These cataclysmic explosions of dying stars are responsible for spreading out heavier elements into space with which a new generation of stars will be born. In 2019, research done with the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope at Mauna Kea enabled the detection of at least 42 supernovae remnants within NGC 3344.
name: NGC 3344

description: The Carina nebula, often called Eta Carinae nebula, is a bright and large nebula in the constellation of Carina. NGC 3372 is one of the largest diffuse nebulae in the night sky and is a very popular target for astrophotographers who are able to image from the Southern hemisphere. The Carina nebula is about four times as large as the famous Orion nebula, and is also brighter!
name: Carina Nebula

description: NGC 3511 and NGC 3513 are a pair of spiral galaxies in the constellation Crater. NGC 3511 is 88,000 light-years across and NGC 3513 is 46,000 light-years across. There is a supermassive black hole weighing a few million solar masses in the center of NGC 3511. The total mass of the stars is estimated to be 10 billion solar masses, which is equivalent to the properties of our own galaxy. The galaxy transforms its gas clouds into stars at a rate of 1 solar mass per year, slightly less than that of the Milky Way. NGC 3513 has a central bar from which the spiral arms extend. They are therefore not directly attached to the center of the galaxy. The bar is made up of many stars.
name: NGC 3511

description: "NGC 3521 is a spiral galaxy located 26 million light-years away from Earth, in the constellation Leo. It is classified as a flocculent (synonym for 'fluffy') galaxy, a type of spiral galaxy which, unlike galaxies with a well-defined spiral architecture, shows patchy and discontinuous spiral arms. We can find a massive, bright, and extremely compact nucleus in the center of the galaxy."
name: NGC 3521

description: Located in the constellation Carina, NGC 3532 is a bright and colorful open cluster counting approximately 150 stars of 7th magnitude or fainter. This grouping of stars is about 300 million years old. This makes the group middle-aged by open star cluster standards. It includes seven red giants and seven white dwarfs.
name: Football Cluster

description:
"NGC3576's nickname finds its origins in the darker clouds of dense gas and dust that resemble the silhouette of the Statue of Liberty in the background of the nebula. 
It is an active region where massive stars are being formed, young stars a few million years old whose strong ultraviolet rays light up the nebula, and dying stars which expel their gas. 
In the sky, it is not far from the well-known Eta Carina nebula. Both nebulae are located a few thousand light-years apart, in the Sagittarius Arm of the Milky Way galaxy."
name: Statue of Liberty Nebula

description: NGC 362 is a fairly shiny globular cluster from the Tucana constellation. Where globular clusters are generally made of older stars than the rest of the stars located elsewhere in the galaxy, NGC 362 is a particular case. This cluster features stars whose age is lower than the age of the average stellar population of the Milky Way. Locating NGC 362 is made easier as the so-called Small Magellanic Cloud (NGC 292 or SMC) is in its vicinity. If NGC 362 and NGC 292 seem to be bound together, it is actually an optical illusion as the globular cluster is 7 times closer to the Earth than is the SMC.
name: NGC 362

description: NGC 3621 is a spiral galaxy in the Hydra constellation. This galaxy the size of the Milky Way is a field galaxy; in other words, it is isolated and does not belong to a galaxy group or cluster. Like M33, it has no central bulge, but only a central black hole. The mass of the latter is estimated to be three million times the mass of the Sun or about 25% less than that of our galaxy. These characteristics lead researchers to believe that the central black hole is in the process of formation and that the bulge will form later.
name: NGC 3621

description:
"NGC 3626, also known as Caldwell 40 is a lenticular galaxy located about 70 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Leo.

The galaxy has a bright nucleus and a well-defined spiral structure with prominent arms.

Observations of NGC 3626 have revealed a number of interesting features. For example, the galaxy has a high rate of star formation, with many bright HII regions visible in its spiral arms. It also has a large-scale magnetic field that is thought to play an important role in shaping its structure and dynamics."
name: Caldwell 40

description: NGC 3766, also called Caldwell 97, is an open star cluster in the Centaurus Constellation located in the Sagittarius-Carina spiral arm of the galaxy. The blue-colored stars in the cluster indicate the presence of young massive stars. More than 190 stars have been found in the cluster, with surface temperatures of up to 20,000°C and 3,000 times brighter than the sun, while more than a dozen rapidly rotating stars surrounded by a disk of material, have also been discovered. Studies estimate the cluster to be 14 million years old. For stars resembling our sun, this is the very beginning of their 10-billion-year life, but for stars ten times more massive than the sun, they have already lived 25% of their life.
name: NGC 3766

description: NGC 3918 is a planetary nebula located in the Centaurus constellation. Its approximate sky position is easier to locate as it follows the direction given by Southern Cross’s minor axis. Because of its small angular size, details in its structure are nearly impossible to see with amateur telescopes and appear as a modest blue-tinted bubble. NGC 3918 is the result of a red-giant exploding star of about 3 solar masses. It has become a white dwarf, its surface temperature nears 140,000 degrees Kelvin. Although its blue shell made of matter and gas was ejected tens of thousands of years ago, astronomers managed to measure the velocity at which this shell is traveling through space. That speed is mind-boggling: 350,000 kilometers an hour.
name: NGC 3918

description: NGC 40 is a planetary nebula located in the constellation Cepheus. It was discovered in 1788 by William Herschel and is also known as the Bow-Tie Nebula.
name: Bow-tie Nebula

description:
"NGC 404, also known as Mirach's Ghost, is a dwarf galaxy located about 10 million light-years away in the constellation Andromeda. It is relatively small, with a diameter of approximately 20,000 light-years, and it has a low surface brightness, making it difficult to observe.

It is a lenticular galaxy without details and very isolated, a little brighter and smaller than the Small Magellanic Cloud."
name: "Mirach's Ghost"

description: The Antennae galaxies, also known as Caldwell 60 and 61 or NGC 4038 and NGC 4039, are a pair of interacting galaxies in the constellation Corvus. The nuclei of the two galaxies are merging. The process is expected to take a few million years, eventually forming a single elliptical galaxy. In the meantime, this approach destabilizes the huge gas clouds of the two galaxies and generates a starburst phase which explains the different very luminous areas. Numerous very hot, bright massive stars also form in these regions and emit the visible blue light shown in the image. The name Antennae comes from the fact that between 300 and 600 million years ago, the two galaxies passed through each other and this first encounter tore off two gigantic tidal tails. These two filaments, consisting of numerous stars that make them shine, resemble insect antennae.
name: Antennae Galaxies

description:
"NGC 4147 is a globular cluster located in the constellation Coma Berenices, approximately 60,000 light-years away from Earth. It was discovered by William Herschel in 1784.

The cluster has a relatively low mass and a small size, with a diameter of only about 25 light-years. It may be one of the oldest globular clusters in the Milky Way, dating back to the early stages of galaxy formation."
name: NGC 4147

description: NGC 4216 is an intermediate spiral galaxy that is seen almost perfectly edge-on. It lies near the center of the Virgo cluster and is one of the brightest and largest members of the group.
name: NGC 4216

description: NGC 4236, also called Caldwell 3, is a barred spiral galaxy located in the Draco constellation. It is a member of the M81 group of galaxies in which we also find M82. The mass of all the stars in this galaxy is estimated at 1 billion times that of the Sun. This value is 60 times smaller than that of our galaxy. With a diameter of 80,000 light-years, NGC 4236 is about 20% smaller than the Milky Way.
name: NGC 4236

description: NGC 4244 is an edge-on galaxy spreading out over 65,000 light-years. Located in the Coma Berenices constellation, it is part of the nearby M94 galactic group located 14 million light-years away: a relatively close distance when considering that most galactic groups are at least twice as far. The special feature of NGC 4244? The plane in which stars are orbiting is perfectly aligned with Earth’s line of sight. Consequently, we can only admire this spiral galaxy from the edge, hence the name ‘Silver Needle Galaxy’.
name: Silver Needle Galaxy

description:
"NGC 4314 is a little-known barred spiral galaxy, part of the galaxy-rich Coma Berenices constellation. Located 40 million light-years away, two noticeable and physically contrasted features make this galaxy really special: a bright barred inner ring - called a nuclear ring - containing a dense population of stars as young as 15 million years and a second outer ring containing stars up to 200 million years old.
Through a telescope, the external ring, in spite of its low brightness, is the most outstanding of the two since its helix shape remains clearly visible."
name: NGC 4314

description: NGC 4372, also known as Caldwell 108, is a globular cluster in the Musca constellation. It is close to the Dark Doodad Nebula. The total mass of the cluster is estimated at 329,000 solar masses. This mass is distributed across no less than 28,000 stars. The stars in the cluster formed 12.54 billion years ago.
name: NGC 4372

description: NGC 4395 is a diffuse spiral galaxy located at a distance of about 14 million light-years in the Canes Venatici constellation. If this constellation is one of the smallest ones in the sky, it displays, however, a rich panel of galaxies which are mainly accessible to amateur telescopes. NGC 4395 is part of them. Despite its low surface brightness, numerous remote bright regions within the galaxy compensate for its lack of overall luminosity. Therefore NGC 4395 belongs to the Magellanic galaxies category by its heterogeneous structure which is reminiscent of the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.
name: NGC 4395

description:
"NGC 4438 is a spiral galaxy located in the Virgo constellation, at 50 million light-years from Earth. It is part of Markarian's Chain.
NGC 4438 has long tidal tails and a very distorted disk. It is classified as a peculiar galaxy because of its unusual shape. The object is situated close to the celestial equator and, as such, it is at least partly visible from both hemispheres in certain times of the year."
name: NGC 4438

description: NGC 4449, also known as Caldwell 21, is an irregular galaxy located in the Canes Venatici constellation. With a size of 23,000 light-years, it is 5 times smaller than the Milky Way and barely twice as big as the Large Magellanic Cloud. This sky object is also considered to be a starburst galaxy. Indeed, because of the interaction with other galaxies, the gas reservoirs collapse on themselves and a huge quantity of new stars are formed. This activity is revealed by the blue colors present on the image.
name: NGC 4449

description: Despite its unusual shape, the Cocoon Galaxy is indeed a galaxy, of the barred spiral type. It is part of the group of galaxies of M106, in the constellation Canes Venatici, the Hunting Dogs. Its particular shape is due to the effect of attraction to a smaller irregular galaxy, NGC 4485.
name: Cocoon Galaxy

description: Discovered by William Herschel in 1785, this barred spiral galaxy is one of the largest in the Virgo cluster. Even though the size of this galactic cluster is about the same as the cluster in which the Milky Way is included, the Virgo cluster itself contains 50 times more galaxies! From the Earth, the galaxy’s disk is nearly seen face-on, allowing us to admire two of its main properties: on the one hand blue outer spiral arms indicate young, bright and warm stars. On the other hand, a yellowish nucleus highlights a rather old and cold stellar population.
name: Lost Galaxy

description: Located about 30 million light-years away from Earth, NGC 4559 is a spiral galaxy belonging to the Coma Berenices constellation that was discovered by astronomer William Herschel in 1785. This galaxy, featuring detailed and colorful structures, is located close to Melotte 111: an open star cluster that may be spotted by the naked eye in a dark-sky location. NGC 4559 has a star formation rate higher than average and is surrounded by a relatively large disk of hydrogen gas. Though only visible in the radio-waves spectrum, this accretion disk would spread 50% further than the galaxy itself. In 2018, astronomers observed anomalies affecting its shape: the hydrogen gas was not rising from NGC 4559 as previously established but instead seems to have been brought by external sources such as the interstellar medium.
name: NGC 4559

description: The Needle galaxy is a great example of a galaxy seen from its edge, and it is the largest visible one! NGC 4565 has a very bright core, and is home to about 240 globular clusters.
name: Needle Galaxy

description: NGC 4567 and NGC 4568 form a pair of galaxies nicknamed the Butterfly Galaxy. Located in the Virgo constellation, these two spiral galaxies are at the start of a process of interaction and fusion even though no distortion and no tidal filaments connecting the two galaxies have yet been observed.
name: Butterfly Galaxies

description: "NGC 457 is an open cluster in Cassiopeia. Two of its stars are very bright, at magnitude +5 and +7, they look like the eyes of an owl, or an extraterrestrial alien. This cluster is not part of Messier's catalog, but is worth observing and photographing!"
name: Owl Cluster

description: NGC 4609 is an open star cluster located in the vicinity of the main star of the Southern Cross constellation. At the end of the ‘60s, three 1-meter class telescopes were used to conclude that the cluster would contain at least 33 stars. The number has, since then, reached 48 thanks to more advanced and modern observations carried out in 1997 at the Siding Spring Observatory in Australia.
name: NGC 4609

description: The Whale is a barred spiral galaxy full of details, seen from its side from our point of view. The Whale galaxy has a small companion, the tiny elliptical galaxy NGC 4627, which is visible just above the Whale. You may also spot another object around: NGC 4656/4657, most often called the Hockey Stick galaxy.
name: Whale Galaxy

description: NGC 4656/4657 is an edge-on barred spiral galaxy located in the Canes Venatici constellation. It is part of a larger galactic group with the Whale galaxy (NGC 4631) being the main member. The latter exerts a strong gravitational force constraining the shape of NGC 4656 in a highly chaotic way. The upper edge of the galaxy shows another scar: a dimmer region seems to be detaching from it. Initially considered as an isolated spiral arm related to the galaxy, recent studies have shown that this anomaly is likely to be a dwarf galaxy captured by NGC 4656.
name: Hockey Stick Galaxy

description: "NGC 4697, otherwise known as Caldwell 52, is an elliptical galaxy in the constellation Virgo (The Virgin) and the most prominent member of the so-called NGC 4697 Group. It was discovered by William Herschel in 1784 and glows with an apparent magnitude of 10.97. The galaxy has an apparent extent of 7.1', which suggests an actual diameter of 83,000 light-years if its distance from Earth is 40 million light-years, although there is some uncertainty about how far away it is. Evidence suggests that a supermassive black hole lies at the center of NGC 4697 of up to 130 million times the mass of the Sun."
name: Caldwell 52

description: NGC 4725 is a spiral galaxy in the Coma Berenices constellation. With an estimated size of 100,000 light-years, it is the same size as our galaxy. It is currently approaching us at a speed of 1,200 km/s, in other words, 8,000 times faster than the fastest train. The galaxy is in interaction with its neighboring galaxy NGC 4747. The result is that the spiral arm of the galaxy is distorted. The galaxy’s matter is attracted to the other galaxy by the force of gravity. In this image, you can also see the spiral galaxy NGC 4712. The latter is located 200 million light-years away from our galaxy, in other words, about five times farther away than NGC 4725.
name: NGC 4725

description: NGC 4755 is a beautiful open cluster in the constellation of Crux. It is one of the youngest clusters known and is home to some of the brightest stars in the Milky Way. The Jewel Box cluster is easily visible to the naked eye.
name: Jewel Box

description: NGC 4833 is a 42-light-year diameter globular cluster, located more than 20,000 light-years away in the direction of the Musca constellation - a neighbor of the well-known Southern Cross constellation. This region of the sky is altered by huge amounts of dust emanating from within the Milky Way galaxy such as the Coalsack dark nebula. These concentrations of interstellar dust act as filters on the light coming from background objects. Stars of NGC 4833 are actually redder than they are supposed to be as this dust is absorbing the blue light - a process widely known by astronomers as interstellar reddening.
name: NGC 4833

description: Berenice’s Hair Cluster, also known as Coma or Caldwell 35, is a cluster of galaxies in the constellation of the same name. More than 1,000 galaxies have been identified in this cluster, most of them elliptical. The total mass of the cluster is thought to be 3 million billion-times that of the Sun! As a result, many of the points observed in the image are not stars but elliptical galaxies located about 320 million light years away, the main ones being NGC 4874 and NGC 4889.
name: "Berenice's Hair Cluster"

description: "Similar in size and shape to the Milky Way, NGC 4945 is a barred spiral galaxy found in the constellation Centaurus. It's the second brightest member of the group of galaxies it is part of, the Centaurus A/M83 Group. NGC 4945 is classified as a Seyfert galaxy, a type of large spiral galaxies characterized by an extremely bright and compact core which is supposed to be home of an active supermassive black hole."
name: NGC 4945

description: "NGC 5005, also known as Caldwell 29, is a magnitude 10.6 spiral galaxy in the northern constellation Canes Venatici (The Hunting Dogs). It's inclined to our line of sight, but in large amateur-sized telescopes it presents a bright nucleus and several dust lanes within its tightly-wound spiral arms. Distance estimates vary considerably but average 70 million light-years from Earth, where its apparent dimension of 5.8' implies an actual diameter of about 120 million light-years. Therefore, NGC 5005 is about 12% larger than our Milky Way. NGC 5033 is a slightly larger spiral galaxy that lies ⅔° southeast of NGC 5005, making a physical pair."
name: Caldwell 29

description: NGC 5033 is a spiral galaxy in the Canes Venatici constellation. With a size of 100,000 light-years, it closely resembles the Milky Way, which it is approaching at a speed of 875 km/s. It does however have a very bright core and a much fainter disk. The gas and dust clouds, and the stars revolve around a center that is offset from the position of the galaxy’s central black hole. This peculiarity is the result of the merger of NGC 5033 with another galaxy during the last billion years. The Hubble Space Telescope has also detected a ring around the center in which new stars are forming.
name: NGC 5033

description: Centaurus A is a bright starburst galaxy that is difficult to see from Northern locations. NGC 5128 is the closest giant galaxy to our Milky Way, and one of the nearest radio galaxies known. Centaurus A is a popular target for amateur astrophotographers located in the Southern hemisphere, as its starburst activity looks very impressive on photos.
name: Centaurus A

description: Best seen from the Southern part of the world, NGC 5139, or Omega Centauri, is the largest, and brightest globular cluster in the night sky. Home to about 10 millions of stars, the cluster is easily visible with the naked eye, and looks very impressive in photographs. Omega Centauri has a mass of 5 million Suns, meaning that it is about 10 times more massive than other usual globular clusters.
name: Omega Centauri

description: NGC 5189, also called IC4274, is a planetary nebula located in the Musca constellation. This planetary nebula is located about 5,500 light-years away from us and is three light-years in size according to the latest data from the Gaia satellite. The shape of this nebula is very peculiar because it looks like a spiral galaxy. You can see a reddish filamentary structure in the shape of an S surrounding blue lobes. This atypical shape is due to the fact that the solar-type star that created the nebula at its death is accompanied by another star. The latter disrupts the expansion of the gas shell.
name: NGC 5189

description: "NGC 5248, otherwise known as Caldwell 45, is a beautiful intermediate spiral galaxy in the southwestern corner of the constellation Boötes (The Herdsman), but it's actually part of the Virgo Cluster. William Herschel discovered NGC 5248 in 1784. It has an apparent magnitude of 10.97 and lies about 55 million light-years from Earth, but its distance is not known with certainty. NGC 5248 has an apparent size of 6.2', which implies an actual diameter of about 100,000 light-years, similar to our own Milky Way."
name: Caldwell 45

description:
"NGC 5281 is a relatively bright open star cluster of the Centaurus constellation and 4,240 light-years distant. It also has the ‘Lacaille I.7’ denomination in honor of its discoverer, Nicolas Louis de Lacaille, a French astronomer who led a scientific expedition in South Africa to map new celestial objects. Lacaille managed to contribute to the astronomy community by releasing a catalog of 42 objects, tens of which were not formerly reported.
According to a 2000 study, NGC 5281 would contain at least 172 members and their motion velocity projected onto the sky map would be 7.57 thousandth of an arcsecond per year. Such an unfamiliar value is extremely low since it would correspond to observing a 12-meter position change of a lunar rover as seen through an Earth-based telescope!"
name: NGC 5281

description: "NGC 5286, also known as Caldwell 84, is a globular cluster in the constellation Centaurus. The cluster is part of the Monoceros Ring, which is a stellar structure that wraps around our galaxy. It is 200,000 light-years long and weighs 100 million solar masses. The cluster is about 12.5 billion years old, making it one of the oldest clusters in the Milky Way. Its mass is estimated to be that of 710,000 Suns. The core of the cluster is believed to contain a black hole with a mass 1,500 to 4,000 times the mass of the Sun. Early in the cluster's life, collisions at the core of the cluster led to the formation within a few million years of a star several hundred times the mass of the Sun. When this star died, a black hole formed. It then grew by capturing matter from its surroundings."
name: NGC 5286

description: Commonly known as the Snowglobe Cluster, NGC 5466 is a magnitude 9.7 globular cluster in the constellation Boötes (The Herdsman) discovered by William Herschel in 1784. It’s often overlooked because it lies a binocular field of view east of spectacular globular Messier 3 in the neighbouring constellation Canes Venatici (The Hunting Dogs). NGC 5466 appears half the size of M3 because it is 1½ times farther away, some 51,800 light-years from Earth. It also lies at a high galactic latitude, almost at right angles to the plane of the Milky Way. The stars of NGC 5466 are incredibly ancient, approximately 13.5 billion years old.
name: NGC 5466

description: NGC 55, also known as Caldwell 72, is a spiral galaxy located in the Sculptor Constellation. NGC 55 only has one spiral arm, whereas the Milky Way has 4. This dwarf galaxy is roughly 60,000 light-years across, making it about half the size of the Milky Way. Caldwell 72 has an estimated mass of 20 billion solar masses, which is about 50 times lighter than the mass of our galaxy. In the sky, this galaxy is in the same region as the Sculptor group of galaxies. However, NGC 55 is not part of this cluster of galaxies because it is located 6.33 million light-years away, twice as close as the other Sculptor galaxies.
name: NGC 55

description:
"NGC 5566, together with NGC 5560 and NGC 5569, are three spiral galaxies in the constellation Virgo. The trio of galaxies are interacting with each other and will eventually merge into a huge elliptical galaxy. Meanwhile, these interactions are already deforming the spiral arms of NGC 5560, which are stretched and distorted by the attraction of NGC 5566.
NGC 5566 is 150,000 light-years across, that is, 50% more than our galaxy. NGC 5560 is 82,000 light-years across. NGC 5569 is the smallest of the galaxies in this trio at only 40,000 light-years across.
The three galaxies are approaching us at a speed of 1,700 km/s. They could therefore circle the earth in 23.5 seconds"
name: NGC 5566

description: NGC 559, also known as Caldwell 8, is an open cluster in the Cassiopeia Constellation. In terms of the Milky Way, the cluster lies close to the spiral arm of Perseus. Its 542 identified stars are about 225 million years old. The most massive stars detected have surface temperatures of about 10,000°C, which is about 5 times higher than the temperature required to melt iron. The stars are 100 brighter than the Sun, putting them in the B9V spectral type.
name: NGC 559

description: The constellation Virgo (The Virgin) is full of galaxies, but NGC 5634 is its only globular cluster, discovered by William Herschel in 1785. It shines with a combined magnitude of 10, has a diameter of almost 5’, and lies about 82,200 light-years from Earth. A bright, magnitude 7.9 orange star, HD 127119, lies 1’ east of the cluster. NGC 5634 was likely once part of the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy (Sag DEG), a small companion of the Milky Way being pulled apart by gravitational tidal forces from our galaxy.
name: NGC 5634

description: "NGC 5694, or Caldwell 66, is a magnitude 10.2 globular cluster in the constellation Hydra (The Sea Serpent) discovered by William Herschel on 22 May 1784. It's one of the remotest globular known in the Milky Way, some 114,100 light-years from Earth. NGC 5694 spans just 3.6' at such a distance, implying an actual diameter of almost 120 light-years. Its stars are also very ancient, some 13.4 billion years old. NGC 5694 travels so fast through the galaxy, greater than the escape velocity of the Milky Way, that it will eventually pass into intergalactic space, never to return."
name: Caldwell 66

description: "NGC 5823, or Caldwell 88, is a 7th-magnitude open cluster in the obscure southern constellation of Circinus (The Drafting Compass), although its northern edge crosses the border into Lupus (The Wolf). Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered it in 1826. NGC 5823 is 3,900 light-years from Earth where its apparent diameter of 12' implies an actual size of almost 14 light-years. Sixth-magnitude open cluster NGC 5822 appears three times larger and lies two Moon widths to the north of NGC 5823; use Singularity's mosaic mode to capture both in the same field of view."
name: Caldwell 88

description: "NGC 5824 is a magnitude 9 globular cluster in the constellation Lupus (The Wolf) discovered by Scottish astronomer James Dunlop in 1826 and independently by American astronomer Edward E. Barnard in 1884. It lies 4.9 degrees northwest of magnitude 3.6 naked-eye star Phi1 Lupi. The cluster appears 6.2' in diameter, implying an actual diameter of 188 light-years at its distance of 104,500 light-years from Earth."
name: NGC 5824

description: "The Ghost Globular is the name used by renowned author and observer Stephen James O'Meara for NGC 5897, a magnitude 8.2 globular cluster in the constellation Libra (The Scales) situated on a line between naked-eye stars Gamma and Sigma Librae. William Herschel discovered it in 1785. NGC 5897 lies about 40,000 light-years from Earth, so its apparent size of 11' corresponds to a true diameter of about 129 light-years."
name: NGC 5897

description: NGC 5907 is a spiral galaxy in the constellation of Draco, about 50 million light-years away from Earth. In the year 2006, astronomers announced the discovery of a tidal stream of gas that surrounds NGC 5907, and is visible in high-quality photographs.
name: Knife Edge Galaxy

description: "NGC 5927 is a magnitude 8 globular cluster in the constellation Lupus (The Wolf) discovered by Scottish astronomer James Dunlop in 1826 and observed in detail by John Herschel eight years later. It lies near of magnitude 3.4 naked-eye star Zeta Lupi, so it is possible to capture both in the same view with Singularity's Mosaic Mode. The cluster appears 6' in diameter, implying an actual diameter of 44 light-years at its distance of 25,100 light-years from Earth."
name: NGC 5927

description:
"In this field of view, which requires patience and time, we have 3 galaxies in the Draco constellation, 2 of which are not very bright. There is NGC 5982, an elliptical galaxy, NGC 5985, a face-on spiral galaxy, and NGC 5981, an edge-on galaxy.
NGC 5982 is the result of the past merger of two approximately equal-size spiral galaxies. The resulting structure is an elliptical galaxy consisting of several shells enveloping a central nucleus. The light of the galaxy is dominated by old stars, some of which are found in 6 billion-year-old globular clusters."
name: NGC 5982

description: "NGC 6025, also known as Caldwell 95, is a beautiful 5th-magnitude open cluster in the constellation Triangulum Australe (Southern Triangle), although its northern edge crosses the border into Norma (The Carpenter's Square). French astronomer Abbé Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille discovered it in 1751-1752 while touring South Africa. NGC 6025 contains more than 100 stars spread over a 14' field, which equates to an actual size of 11 light-years at the cluster's distance of 2,700 light-years."
name: Caldwell 95

description: "The obscure southern constellation Norma (The Carpenter's Square) is where you will find NGC 6067, a beautiful and bright (magnitude 5.6) open star cluster discovered by Scottish astronomer James Dunlop in 1826. Some 13' in apparent size and 4,600 light-years from Earth, its actual diameter is about 17 light-years. NGC 6067 is such a beautiful object with stars of contrasting colors that renowned observer Stephen James O'Meara described it as one of the sky's most stunning open star clusters, a rewarding sight in all apertures from binoculars to large telescopes."
name: NGC 6067

description:
"NGC 6087, also known as Caldwell 89, is an open cluster in the Norma constellation. The cluster currently has 251 members, the brightest of which is the yellow supergiant S Normae. This star is 2,800 times brighter than the Sun. It is also 6.3 times more massive. S Normae is a Cepheid star. So its magnitude varies from 6.12 to 6.77 over a period of 9.75 days. 
The stars in the cluster formed 100 million years ago."
name: NGC 6087

description: Located in the little-known Apus constellation, NGC 6101 is a 13 million year old globular cluster. Situated 48,000 light-years away from Earth, this cluster is even nearer to the center of the Milky Way than it is to Earth and it is thought to come from a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way: the Canis Major dwarf galaxy.
name: NGC 6101

description:
"NGC 613 is a barred spiral galaxy located 67 million light-years away in the southern constellation of Sculptor. Even though the two-thirds of the spiral galaxies making the Universe are thought to be barred, NGC 613 has the peculiarity of having such a strong central barred region that its central ring is elongated like an ellipse.
Barred spiral galaxies feature higher concentrations of gas than standard spiral ones as they form an active star-forming region at their core. Nevertheless, NGC 613 does not comply with this rule: its central bar forms less stars than its surrounding regions. Such a scenario can be explained because of greater collision velocity of the molecular clouds in the central zone than in the outer spiral arms. This rise of matter’s collision rate within the bar region would prevent larger molecular clouds from forming new stars."
name: NGC 613

description: "Commonly known as the Little Pincushion, NGC 6134 is a magnitude 7.2 open cluster in the southern constellation Norma (The Carpenter's Square). Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered it in 1826. NGC 6134 lies about 4,100 light-years from Earth and is situated on the border of what seems to be a dark cloud."
name: NGC 6134

description: NGC 6139 is a rich and dense globular cluster of the Milky Way, located approximately 35,000 light-years away from Earth in the constellation Scorpius. It is home to an aging population of stars.
name: NGC 6139

description: NGC 6164 and NGC 6165 form an emission nebula in the Norma constellation. About 4,000 light-years away from Earth, the gas in the nebula is heated by the star HD 148937 located at the center of the structure. Although it resembles a planetary nebula, it is in fact another type of object because the central star is young (4 million years) and massive (60 solar masses) whereas the planetary nebulae are formed by old Sun-like stars at the end of their life (10 billion years). The central star underwent two violent eruptions, 600,000 years ago and 1.2 million years ago, ejecting between 1.5 and 12 solar masses of matter. The nebula is not spherical because the material would have mainly been ejected along the star’s north and south pole.
name: NGC 6164

description: NGC 6188 is an emission nebula located 4,000 light-years away from us in the Ara constellation. This nebula is part of a molecular cloud with a mass equivalent to more than 8,000 solar masses and in which a new generation of stars is forming. The red hues in the image are due to the edges of the cloud absorbing intense UV light emitted by the young star cluster NGC 6193, also visible in the image. The matter expelled by the massive stars in this cluster sculpts and tears the gas cloud, giving it its particular shape. The dark and black areas are the regions of the cloud that are still cold and emit no light. The very young star cluster NGC 6193, also known as Caldwell 93, is three million years old and contains more than 550 stars, some of which weigh more than 10 times the mass of the Sun. In a few million years, the most massive stars will turn into supernovas.
name: Rim Nebula

description: NGC 6229 is a globular cluster located in the Hercules constellation. It is one of the globular clusters located in the outer reaches of our galaxy and one of the most distant known from the Earth. The stars in this cluster were formed 12 billion years ago, which is 7.5 billion years before our Sun. An analysis of the composition of different stars in the cluster showed that the stars were not all formed at the same time and that there would have been two formation periods. The origin of the cluster is not fully determined and it could have formed in another galaxy before being captured by the Milky Way.
name: NGC 6229

description: NGC 6231, also known as Caldwell 76 or the Northern Jewel Box because it resembles NGC 4755, is a very young few million-year-old open cluster located in the Scorpius constellation. It contains about 7,500 stars, equivalent to half of the Sumatran orangutan population. The stars in the cluster are distributed in a broad range of mass. Accordingly, there are a hundred or so stars that weigh more than 10 times the mass of the Sun, several hundred stars that weigh a few solar masses, and several thousand stars lighter than the Sun. The stars in this cluster are approaching us at 22 km/s, which is slightly faster than the speed of the Voyager 1 probe (16.6 km/s).
name: Northern Jewel Box

description: "From the Southern Hemisphere, as autumn segues into winter during May and June, the constellation of Scorpius (The Scorpion) is highest in the northern sky at midnight. It's one of the few constellations that doesn't need a great imagination to visualize in the sky, with a row of prominent stars shaped like a question mark delineating its tail and 'sting'. Close to the center of the curving tail lies magnitude 8 open star cluster NGC 6259. It appears 14' in diameter, which at its 3,400 light-year distance from Earth corresponds to an actual size of 14' light-years."
name: NGC 6259

description: "NGC 6296 is a magnitude 14.2 spiral galaxy in the constellation Ophiuchus (The Serpent Handler), discovered by German astronomer Albert Marth in 1863. It is observable from every inhabited place on Earth because it lies close to the celestial equator. NGC 6296 lies some 329 million light-years from Earth, so its apparent size of 0.9' corresponds to a true diameter of about 86,100 light-years."
name: NGC 6296

description: Located at a distance of about 5,500 light-years toward the galactic center, the informally named Cat’s Paw is a nebula rich in gas and dust, long known to contain very massive young stars. Their presence causes the surrounding hydrogen gas to glow red.
name: Cat’s Paw Nebula

description: "NGC 6342 is a globular cluster of the Ophiuchus constellation. Visible from both Hemispheres, it is located not too far from the Lagoon nebula and more precisely in the same area as the Dark horse nebula. Its low extent and its low brightness compared to other globular clusters are caused by its great distance to the solar system: 28,000 light-years. NGC 6342 is thus 4.3 times closer to the center of the Milky Way than to the Sun. Globular clusters are to the Milky Way what comets are to the solar system: they were formed at the first moments of the galaxy's birth, inside a hot and dense nebula. Their observations enable us to trace back the dynamics of our own galaxy and follow the chemical elements being spread out into space."
name: NGC 6342

description:
"NGC 6352, also known as Caldwell 81, is a globular cluster in the Ara constellation. At 12.6 billion years old, it is most likely composed like most globular clusters of two star populations. The second population most likely formed 275 million years after the first one in the residues of gas chemically enriched by the massive stars of the first generation that died.
The mass of the cluster is estimated to be 61,000 solar masses."
name: NGC 6352

description: NGC 6356 is another globular cluster of the Ophiuchus constellation. It is, however, brighter and denser than its neighbor NGC 6342. This region of the night sky is one of the richest in terms of star clusters as it benefits from pointing towards the center of the Milky Way galaxy. In addition to NGC 6342, NGC 6346 has a more popular and brighter second neighbor as well: the cluster M9 or NGC 6333.
name: NGC 6356

description: Located in Scorpius and spanning about 400 light-years, the Lobster Nebula forms a complex cloud of gas, dark dust, stars still forming, and newly born stars with strong interactions between interstellar winds, radiation pressures, magnetic fields and gravity. The overall blue glow near the inner star-forming region is the result of the emission of ionized hydrogen gas.
name: Lobster Nebula

description: "NGC 6366 is a 9th-magnitude globular cluster in the constellation Ophiuchus (The Serpent Handler) discovered by German astronomer August Winnecke in 1860. It lies half a Moon's width to the east of naked-eye star 47 Ophiuchi and in the same binocular field of view as 7th-magnitude globular cluster M14 to the northeast, so why not use Singularity's mosaic mode to capture all three? NGC 6366 lies 11,700 light-years from Earth and appears 13' in diameter, implying an actual size of 44 light-years."
name: NGC 6366

description: "NGC 6380 is an 11th-magnitude globular cluster in the constellation Scorpius (The Scorpion), with the unusual distinction of having three independent discoverers! The first was Scottish astronomer James Dunlop in 1826, and it was found again by English polymath John Herschel eight years later. Lost once more, Armenian-Mexican astronomer Marie Paris Pişmiş de Recillas rediscovered it in 1959 and grandly christened it Tonantzintla 1. NGC 6380 lies about 35,500 light-years from Earth, where its apparent size of 3.9' implies an actual diameter of 40 light-years."
name: NGC 6380

description: "NGC 6388 is a conspicuous sixth-magnitude globular cluster with a bright central core in the constellation Scorpius (The Scorpion), discovered by Scottish astronomer James Dunlop from Australia in 1826. NGC 6388 lies three-and-a-half Moon widths below (as seen from the Northern Hemisphere) Sargas, the southernmost conspicuous star in the celestial scorpion's tail. The globular cluster lies about 32,000 light-years from Earth, where its apparent size of 6.2' suggests an actual diameter of around 57 light-years."
name: NGC 6388

description: NGC 6397 is, right after Messier 4, the nearest globular cluster to Earth, at a distance of only 7,200 light-years (7,000 for M4). NGC 6397 is also the nearest cluster to us that has undergone core-collapse. A total of about 20 globular clusters are known to have had experienced that.
name: NGC 6397

description: "NGC 6401 is a 9th-magnitude globular cluster in the constellation Ophiuchus (The Serpent Handler) discovered by William Herschel in 1784. William and his son John couldn't resolve the object into individual stars using the telescopes of their time, so they mistakenly thought it was a nebula. The Hubble Space Telescope revealed that NGC 6401 is composed of thousands of stars and lies about 35,000 light-years from Earth, where its apparent size of 1.5' suggests an actual diameter of 15 light-years."
name: NGC 6401

description: Located in one of the most populated areas of the sky, Sagittarius, NGC 6440 is an old globular cluster formed 13 billion years ago and located 26,000 light-years away. It is orbiting around the bulge of the Milky Way and one thinks it is now in a dynamically evolved state so that stars have already interacted together. At this stage, it is almost impossible to get back to the initial trajectories of the stars when the cluster was about to be formed.
name: NGC 6440

description: "NGC 6522 is a 9th-magnitude globular cluster in the constellation Sagittarius (The Archer) discovered by William Herschel in 1784. It appears close to the Galactic Centre in a region of space known as Baade's (after astronomer Walter Baade) Window, where a low concentration of interstellar dust gives us a clear view of the Milky Way. NGC 6522 is composed of thousands of stars around 12 billion years old and lies about 25,000 light-years from Earth, where its apparent size of 3.9' suggests an actual diameter of 28 light-years. Another globular cluster, 10th-magnitude NGC 6528, lies half a lunar diameter to the east."
name: NGC 6522

description: The Red Spider is a bipolar planetary nebula located in the Sagittarius constellation. In its center lies a white dwarf; stars residual shape at the end of their life. The very powerful and extremely hot winds produced by the white dwarf give the nebula its two-lobed shape, with winds estimated to blow at 300 km per second.
name: Red Spider Nebula

description: "NGC 6539 is an 8th-magnitude globular cluster with dual constellation citizenship: its centre lies in Serpens Caput (The Serpent's Head), but its western edge crosses the border into Ophiuchus (The Serpent Handler). Danish astronomer Theodor Brorsen discovered it in 1856. NGC 6539 is about 25,400 light-years from Earth, where its apparent size of 7.9' corresponds to an actual diameter of 58 light-years. Tenth-magnitude globular cluster IC 1276 lies three Moon-widths to the east-northeast of NGC 6539; try using Singularity's mosaic mode to capture both."
name: NGC 6539

description: "NGC6541 is a large and bright globular cluster located in Corona Australis, a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere. It is a concentration of about 150,000 stars which form a sphere of a hundred light-years in diameter. The cluster's heart is so dense that it is not possible to distinguish the stars, it therefore appears as a fuzzy whole."
name: NGC 6541

description: "NGC 6543, also known as the Cat's Eye Nebula, is a planetary nebula with a magnitude of 8.80 and a small angular diameter, 3,000 light-years distant and currently located near the ecliptic north pole."
name: "Cat's Eye Nebula"

description: "NGC 6546 is an 8th-magnitude open star cluster in the constellation of Sagittarius (The Archer). You can be forgiven for overlooking it because it lies close to two prominent objects: Messier 8 (The Lagoon Nebula) and Messier 20 (The Trifid Nebula). By using Singularity's Mosaic Mode, you can capture all three objects simultaneously! Astronomers believe that NGC 6546 is about 3,100 light-years from Earth, where its 13' apparent size equates to an actual diameter of almost 12 light-years."
name: NGC 6546

description: "NGC 6553 is an 8th-magnitude globular cluster in the constellation Sagittarius (The Archer) located four Moon widths southeast of the unmissable Lagoon Nebula (Messier 8), so you could capture both using Singularity's mosaic mode. William Herschel discovered NGC 6553 in 1784. Some 19,600 light-years from Earth, its apparent size of 4.5' suggests an actual diameter of 26 light-years. Astronomers believe that NGC 6553 underwent more than two periods of star formation."
name: NGC 6553

description: "NGC 6558 is an eighth-magnitude globular cluster in the constellation Sagittarius (The Archer) located three Moon widths southeast of Alnasl (Gamma2 Sagittarii), the naked-eye star representing the “spout” of the constellation's “Teapot” asterism. William Herschel discovered NGC 6558 in 1784. Some 24,000 light-years from Earth, its apparent size of 4.2' suggests an actual diameter of 29 light-years. Astronomers believe that NGC 6558 could contain up to half a million stars."
name: NGC 6558

description: "Once you have imaged the Lagoon Nebula (Messier 8) and the Trifid Nebula (Messier 20) in the constellation Sagittarius (The Archer), you may care to look 1½° to their east and locate NGC 6559, a striking object combining a blue reflection nebula, a red emission nebula, and dark obscuring dust. It lies about 5,000 light-years from Earth. NGC 6559 borders on IC 4685, a bright nebula that is somewhat larger, approximately 10' x 8'. Try using Singularity's mosaic mode to capture both."
name: NGC 6559

description: "NGC 6569 is an eighth-magnitude globular cluster in the constellation of Sagittarius (The Archer) located four Moon widths southeast of Alnasl (Gamma2 Sagittarii), the naked-eye star representing the spout of the constellation's Teapot asterism. William Herschel discovered NGC 6569 from England in 1784. About 35,500 light-years from Earth, its apparent size of 6.4' suggests an actual diameter of 66 light-years. Astronomers believe that NGC 6569 is about 12 billion years old."
name: NGC 6569

description:
"NGC 663, also known as Caldwell 10, is an open cluster in the Cassiopeia constellation. The Gaia Mission identified 468 stars in this cluster. The hottest of them has a surface temperature of almost 13,000 degrees, which is more than twice the temperature of the Sun's surface and 13 times that required to melt gold. And the coldest one it was possible to measure has a temperature equal to that of the Sun. These stars and their companions formed 30 million years ago. 
The cluster also contains at least 24 Be-type stars. A distinguishing feature of these stars is that they spin very quickly on themselves, faster than 300 km/s, and are consequently heavily flattened."
name: NGC 663

description: "NGC 6624 is a 7th-magnitude globular cluster located in the teapot-shaped asterism of the constellation Sagittarius (The Archer), discovered by William Herschel in 1784. It lies less than two full Moon widths to the lower-left for Northern Hemisphere observers (upper-right south of the equator) of the naked-eye star Delta Sagittarii. Astronomers believe that NGC 6624 is about 25,800 light-years from Earth, where its apparent size of 8.8' translates to an actual diameter of 66 light-years."
name: NGC 6624

description: NGC 6633, also called the Captain Hook Cluster, is an open cluster in the Ophiuchus constellation. In the sky, it is a large cluster that is nearly the size of the full Moon. The latest studies conducted with Gaia data show that the cluster contains at least 100 stars and that it is about 700 million years old. While Sun-like stars are at less than 10% of their life, stars larger than five solar masses are already dead.
name: Captain Hook Cluster

description:
"NGC 6709, also known as The Flying Unicorn Cluster, is an open cluster in the Aquila constellation. It is around 150 million years old, about the same as the Pleiades. It contains 305 stars according to the last census performed by the Gaia Mission, in other words, ten times less than the Pleiades cluster. The hottest stars in the cluster have surface temperatures of 14,000 degrees.

The stars in the cluster are moving towards us at a speed of 7.8 km/s or 28,000 km/h. This is ten times faster than the cruising speed of the JWST when it was traveling to its observation mission position."
name: Flying Unicorn Cluster

description:
"NGC 6712 is a small globular cluster situated in the fifth smallest constellation: Scutum. Like a lot of other globular clusters within this area of the sky, it also belongs to the galactic bulge.
Astrophysicists have recently discovered that NGC 6712 would have, at multiple times, been in interaction with the Milky Way’s bulge leading to a dispersion of its stellar members on its course. Because of these recurrent encounters, some stars would have been disseminated in the orbital plane of the galaxy and would head toward its core."
name: NGC 6712

description: NGC 6723, also known as the Chandelier Cluster, is a globular cluster in the Sagittarius constellation. In the Milky Way, the cluster is located in the galactic bulge less than 3,300 light-years from the center of the Galaxy, or eight times closer than we are to the galactic center. It is 12.5 billion years old. The mass of all the stars is estimated to be 172,000 times that of the Sun. It basically consists of old, low-mass stars, that is, with masses within the range of the Sun or even lower. Only 36% of the stars it contains formed during the first star-burst event, the rest formed later, during a second star-forming event.
name: Chandelier Cluster

description:
"NGC 6726 is a reflection nebula in the Corona Australis constellation. This gigantic cloud of gas and fine dust reflects the blue light from the stars in the nearby cluster on its surface. In the latter, only two stars are observable in visible light, R Coronae Australis (R CrA) and T Coronae Australis (T CrA). The 12 other stars in the cluster are buried in the gas cloud and are only visible because of their infrared signature. We should also note the presence of reflection nebula NGC 6729. Dust and gas surrounding R CrA reflects a portion of the light emitted by the star.
R CrA is in fact a binary system that consists of a star with a mass of 3.5 solar masses and a companion with a mass of 2.3 solar masses. The stars orbit each other in 45 years. The system is estimated to be 1 million years old."
name: NGC 6726

description: "Magnitude 8.3 spiral galaxy NGC 6744, also known as Caldwell 101, is the brightest example in the southern constellation Pavo (The Peacock). Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered it in 1826. About 30 million light-years from Earth, astronomers believe it closely resembles how our Milky Way would look from afar.
